DP-Rec: Towards Dynamic Patching for Efficient Long-Sequence Recommendation

Conference: 20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems; September 27-October 02, 2026; Minneapolis, MN, USA20th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys ’26), September 27-October 02, 2026, Minneapolis, MN, USADOI: 10.1145/3773078.3831823ISBN: 979-8-4007-2284-4/2026/09CCS: Computing methodologies Machine learningCCS: Information systems Recommender systemsCCS: Computing methodologies Knowledge representation and reasoningCCS: Information systems Temporal data
Dwipam Katariya Note: Core Contributors Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, McLean, VA, USA , Thomas Caputo Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, McLean, VA, USA , Akshat Shreemali Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, New York, NY, USA , Juan Manuel Origgi Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, New York, NY, USA , Nikita Seleznev Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, Boston, MA, USA , Pranab Mohanty Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, Seattle, WA, USA , Kalanand Mishra Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, San Jose, CA, USA , Nam Nguyen Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, New York, NY, USA and James Montgomery Affiliation: Capital One, AI Foundations, McLean, VA, USA
© cc
Abstract.

Transformers have redefined sequential recommendation by effectively modeling dynamic user behaviors and long-range dependencies. However, they remain inherently inefficient: standard architectures operate at a fixed rate, allocating comparable computation to every item in a user’s history regardless of its information content. This leads to prohibitive computational overhead on long sequences and increased sensitivity to behavioral noise. To address this, practitioners often resort to lossy sequence compression, staged modeling, or truncation. This limits the model’s ability to leverage the full context of long histories during inference. Inspired by the recent success of Byte Latent Transformer, we propose DP-Rec, a dynamic latent patching architecture for recommendation. DP-Rec shifts from item-level modeling to patch-level modeling by segmenting interaction sequences using contrastive entropy surprise to identify informative behavioral boundaries. A lightweight patch encoder compresses these temporally contextualized segments into a reduced set of dynamic latent behavior vectors, which are then processed by a larger latent transformer and decoded for next-item prediction. Extensive experiments show that, under constrained computational budgets, DP-Rec scales effectively to long sequences and achieves a superior efficiency–accuracy trade-off over both non-compressed and fixed-size compression baselines.

Keywords: 
personalization, long user sequence modeling, transformers, recommender systems

1. Introduction

Modern recommendation systems (RecSys) are undergoing a paradigm shift, moving from traditional feature-based architectures toward generative sequential models capable of processing long user behavior histories. These extended contexts are critical for capturing multifaceted user preferences such as long-term seasonality and recurring interests, which are often discarded by shorter lookback windows or static user embeddings (Zhai et al., 2024; Chai et al., 2025; He et al., 2023; YongjiWu et al., 2021; Chitlangia et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b). Further, scaling sequence length in tandem with other parameters is essential to avoid performance plateaus (Guo et al., 2024). Beyond raw performance gains, larger models are inherently more "sample-efficient," as they extract a higher volume of useful information from individual training examples than smaller models (Zhang et al., 2024a; Zivic et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2024). However, the scalability of Transformer-based architectures is fundamentally constrained by the quadratic computational and memory complexity, denoted as O⁡(N2​d)O(N^{2}d), of the self-attention mechanism relative to sequence length NN and embedding dimension dd (Vaswani et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2025b). In industrial settings, where inference must be executed for every impression within a user session, this burden is often exacerbated by the inclusion of rich item attributes (e.g., categories, brands, and textual descriptions) (Zhai et al., 2024; Katariya et al., 2024; Xia et al., 2025). To mitigate this, practitioners often resort to lossy sequence compression such as embeddings (Katariya et al., 2025; Pancha et al., 2022) or staged modeling. Representative industrial solutions include TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024), which employs hierarchical clustering to compress life-cycle behaviors. Recent works such as LONGER (Chai et al., 2025) have introduced token-merging schemes to compress sequence lengths. However, these methods often rely on fixed heuristics or static partitioning schemes that fail to account for the varying information density of user behavior. We argue that such compression is inherently dependent on information density; naively merging tokens based on a global length or fixed rate is sub-optimal for the varied rhythms of human behavior, requiring dynamic compression solutions as shown in Figure 1. Dynamic compression strategies have recently demonstrated significant potential across diverse sequential domains (Pagnoni et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2026a; Wu et al., 2026b). Specifically, the Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) (Pagnoni et al., 2025) uses a Perceiver-style architecture (Jaegle et al., 2021) for dynamic sequence patching. While BLT establishes the advantage of adaptive, entropy-based patching over static (fixed-vocabulary) tokenization, it derives boundaries from a full next-token softmax that is inexpensive over its 256-symbol byte vocabulary but becomes prohibitive at the million-item vocabularies of production recommender systems. Similarly, PatchTST (Nie et al., 2022) utilizes patching mechanisms to capture local semantic patterns in multivariate time-series data. Despite its success in other fields, dynamic patching has yet to be investigated within the context of RecSys. We argue that a tailored latent architecture is essential to capture the idiosyncratic behavioral dynamics of recommendation data, and introduce DP-Rec, which adapts dynamic latent patching for sequential recommendation. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    To our knowledge, we are the first to establish the viability of dynamic latent patching for sequential recommendation. Across KuaiRand, ML-1M, and ML-10M-L, DP-Rec achieves Pareto-superior trade-offs, delivering either higher inference efficiency under matched accuracy, or higher accuracy within a fixed computational budget.

  • •

    Dynamic Contrastive Patching: We introduce Contrastive Entropy Surprise, a lightweight surrogate for Shannon entropy that resolves the computational intractability of full-vocabulary softmax in recommendations, while providing the dynamic boundary adaptability missing in static models like LONGER (Chai et al., 2025). This formulation demonstrates a propensity to align boundaries with shifts in interaction patterns rather than uniform positions, effectively grouping thematically coherent interaction "bursts".

  • •

    Temporal-Aware Behavioral Context: We incorporate inter-event temporal signals as first-class features within the patching mechanism. By leveraging interaction rhythms and temporal gaps alongside item-ID transitions, DP-Rec establishes temporal dynamics as an important determinant of behavioral context to detect informative segment boundaries.

2. DP-Rec

DP-Rec follows the high-level latent patching paradigm of BLT (Pagnoni et al., 2025) and Perceiver (Jaegle et al., 2021), but adapts the architecture for sequential recommendation. Given a raw interaction sequence of item IDs and Unix timestamps, the behavioral boundary detector identifies patch boundaries used by the temporal local encoder to compress low-surprisal, variable-length segments into latent patch representations. The temporal latent transformer processes these patches, which a local decoder then projects back to item-level states for next-item prediction (Figure 2). Formally, DP-Rec maps a raw interaction sequence to next-item scores through four stages:

Boundaries:   𝐬u→fbbd,Alg. 1(𝚪,𝒫)\displaystyle\mathbf{s}_{u}\xrightarrow{\,f_{\mathrm{bbd}},\ \text{Alg.~\ref{alg:threshold_optimization}}\,}(\boldsymbol{\Gamma},\mathcal{P})
Encode:   𝒫→fenc{𝐳m}m=1M\displaystyle\mathcal{P}\xrightarrow{\,f_{\mathrm{enc}}\,}\{\mathbf{z}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}
Latent:   {𝐳m}→flatent{𝐠m}m=1M\displaystyle\{\mathbf{z}_{m}\}\xrightarrow{\,f_{\mathrm{latent}}\,}\{\mathbf{g}_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}
Decode:   {𝐠m}→fdec{𝐨t}→y^u,t+1\displaystyle\{\mathbf{g}_{m}\}\xrightarrow{\,f_{\mathrm{dec}}\,}\{\mathbf{o}_{t}\}\rightarrow\hat{y}_{u,t+1}

where the boundary detector (fbbdf_{\mathrm{bbd}}) scores contrastive surprise and Algorithm 1 turns it into boundaries 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma} and patches 𝒫\mathcal{P}; the temporal local encoder (fencf_{\mathrm{enc}}) compresses each patch into a latent 𝐳m\mathbf{z}_{m}; the temporal latent Transformer (flatentf_{\mathrm{latent}}) models inter-patch dependencies as 𝐠m\mathbf{g}_{m}; and the local decoder (fdecf_{\mathrm{dec}}) projects back to event states 𝐨t\mathbf{o}_{t} for scoring.

2.1. Temporal Rotary Positional Embeddings (Time-RoPE)

To encode interaction rhythms, we adapt Rotary Positional Embeddings (Su et al., 2024) to absolute timestamps TtT_{t}. For a latent vector 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the transformation ℛ⁡(𝐱,Tt)\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x},T_{t}) rotates d/2d/2 dimension pairs in the query-key space:

(1) ℛ⁡(𝐱,Tt)=𝐱⊙cos⁡(𝚯​Tt)+𝐱~⊙sin⁡(𝚯​Tt),\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x},T_{t})=\mathbf{x}\odot\cos(\boldsymbol{\Theta}T_{t})+\tilde{\mathbf{x}}\odot\sin(\boldsymbol{\Theta}T_{t}),

where 𝐱~\tilde{\mathbf{x}} denotes the vector obtained by rotating each (x2​i−1,x2​i)(x_{2i-1},x_{2i}) pair by 90∘90^{\circ}, i.e., x~2​i−1=−x2​i,x~2​i=x2​i−1\tilde{x}_{2i-1}=-x_{2i},\ \tilde{x}_{2i}=x_{2i-1}, and 𝚯={θi=10000−2i/d}i=1d/2\boldsymbol{\Theta}=\{\theta_{i}=10000^{-2i/d}\}_{i=1}^{d/2} are the inverse frequencies. This makes the attention score between two interactions at times TtT_{t} and Tt′T_{t^{\prime}} a function of their time lag (Tt−Tt′)(T_{t}-T_{t^{\prime}}), giving the boundary detector, local and latent Transformers a continuous, lag-aware sense of behavioral timing.

2.2. Behavioral Boundary Detection

To capture behavioral transitions (such as shifts in user intent or interaction rhythm), we employ a lightweight boundary detector that identifies patch boundaries prior to the primary recommendation model. While Byte-Latent Transformers (Pagnoni et al., 2025) derive boundaries from full-vocabulary next-token entropy, this approach is computationally prohibitive in sequential recommendation due to the massive item vocabulary |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|. Consequently, we utilize a tractable surrogate based on contrastive next-item surprise.

The detector encodes the interaction sequence using a lightweight causal Transformer architecture featuring sliding-window attention and Time-RoPE applied to centered timestamps Δ​Tt=Tt−T1\Delta T_{t}=T_{t}-T_{1}, where T1T_{1} is the timestamp of the first event in the sequence. Let 𝐛t∈ℝdbbd\mathbf{b}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{bbd}}} denote the detector’s hidden state at step tt. The detector is a self-contained module, pre-trained then frozen, with its own parameters and item embeddings at a small hidden size dbbdd_{\mathrm{bbd}} (set to 88 in our experiments); within this subsection 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t} and 𝐞v\mathbf{e}_{v} denote these detector-internal representations, distinct from the recommendation embeddings (∈ℝd\in\mathbb{R}^{d}) used for scoring in Eq. 4. To estimate surprise, we define a binary contrastive objective utilizing the ground-truth next item vt+1v_{t+1} and a sampled negative item vt−v_{t}^{-}. The contrastive surprise score ϕu,t\phi_{u,t} is calculated as:

(2) ϕu,t=−pu,t+​log⁡pu,t+−pu,t−​log⁡pu,t−,\phi_{u,t}=-p^{+}_{u,t}\log p^{+}_{u,t}-p^{-}_{u,t}\log p^{-}_{u,t},

where

(3) pu,t+=exp⁡(𝐛t⊤​𝐞vt+1)exp⁡(𝐛t⊤​𝐞vt+1)+exp⁡(𝐛t⊤​𝐞vt−),pu,t−=1−pu,t+.p^{+}_{u,t}=\frac{\exp(\mathbf{b}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v_{t+1}})}{\exp(\mathbf{b}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v_{t+1}})+\exp(\mathbf{b}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}^{-}})},\qquad p^{-}_{u,t}=1-p^{+}_{u,t}.

A high ϕu,t\phi_{u,t} indicates that the model assigns roughly equal probability to the positive and negative item, signaling a behavioral boundary.

Boundary selection is formulated as an Adaptive Threshold Optimization (Algorithm 1), where a global threshold τ\tau is derived from the empirical surprise distribution to yield binary boundary indicators 𝚪\boldsymbol{\Gamma}.

Contextual Calibration

The optimization context varies by phase: we utilize mini-batch distributions (B>1B>1) during training and independent sequence distributions (B=1B=1) during inference. We establish a combinatorial lemma (see supplementary material for details), which characterizes this behavior; notably, batch-level calibration allows high-entropy sequences to “borrow” capacity from lower-entropy sequences within the same mini-batch. As illustrated in Figure 3, increasing the batch size introduces higher variance in per-sequence patch counts while maintaining the target mean. To ensure deterministic computational control and consistent evaluation, we employ per-sequence thresholding for all validation and test phases. We further note that while ties in surprise scores ϕu,t\phi_{u,t} may lead to minor deviations from the exact cardinality M^\hat{M}, the procedure serves as a robust practical mechanism for behavioral compression across varying sequence lengths.

2.3. Temporal Local Encoder

The local patch encoder transforms event-level sequences into compressed latent representations. We first compute event states 𝐇=[𝐡1,…,𝐡N]\mathbf{H}=[\mathbf{h}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{h}_{N}] via a lightweight causal Transformer fencf_{\mathrm{enc}} utilizing sliding-window attention and Time-RoPE applied to centered timestamps Δ​Tt=Tt−T1\Delta T_{t}=T_{t}-T_{1}.

For each behavioral patch Pm=[lm,rm]P_{m}=[l_{m},r_{m}], an initial latent patch query 𝐳m(0)\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(0)} is constructed via global max pooling over event states:

𝐳m(0)=Winit​(maxt∈Pm⁡𝐡t).\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(0)}=W_{\mathrm{init}}\left(\max_{t\in P_{m}}\mathbf{h}_{t}\right).

These queries are iteratively refined through LencL_{\mathrm{enc}} patch-restricted cross-attention layers, where latent representations act as queries and event states serve as keys and values:

𝐳m(ℓ)=𝐳m(ℓ−1)+CrossAttn⁡(WQ​𝐳m(ℓ−1),{WK​𝐡t,WV​𝐡t}t∈Pm).\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(\ell-1)}+\mathrm{CrossAttn}\left(W_{Q}\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(\ell-1)},\{W_{K}\mathbf{h}_{t},W_{V}\mathbf{h}_{t}\}_{t\in P_{m}}\right).

After LencL_{\mathrm{enc}} layers, the final representation 𝐳m=𝐳m(Lenc)\mathbf{z}_{m}=\mathbf{z}_{m}^{(L_{\mathrm{enc}})} serves as the input latent representation for patch PmP_{m} to the Temporal Latent Transformer.

2.4. Temporal Latent Transformer

Given the latent patch representations 𝐳1,…,𝐳M\mathbf{z}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{z}_{M}, the temporal latent Transformer models dependencies across behavioral patches autoregressively. We use a causal patch-level Transformer, where each patch attends only to previous patches and the current patch.

Unlike the local encoder, where time is defined at the event level, the temporal latent Transformer uses a single temporal anchor per patch. For a patch Pm=[lm,rm]P_{m}=[l_{m},r_{m}], we preserve its patch-end timestamp TrmT_{r_{m}} and use the last centered event time in that patch, Δ​Trm\Delta T_{r_{m}}, in Time-RoPE. Thus, each latent patch is temporally anchored by the time of its final event.

The temporal latent Transformer computes:

𝐠1,…,𝐠M=flatent​(𝐳1,…,𝐳M,Δ​Tr1,…,Δ​TrM),\mathbf{g}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{g}_{M}=f_{\mathrm{latent}}\!\left(\mathbf{z}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{z}_{M};\,\Delta T_{r_{1}},\dots,\Delta T_{r_{M}}\right),

where 𝐠m∈ℝd\mathbf{g}_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the inter-patch representation, and Time-RoPE is applied in patch-level self-attention using these patch-level temporal anchors.

Because the temporal latent Transformer operates on the compressed patch sequence rather than the full interaction history, its cost scales with the number of patches MM rather than the raw sequence length NN.

2.5. Local Decoder

The local decoder projects patch representations back to event-level states for scoring. It reverses the encoder’s cross-attention roles (Pagnoni et al., 2025), using event states as queries and patch representations 𝐠m\mathbf{g}_{m} as keys and values. At layer ℓ∈{1,…,Ldec}\ell\in\{1,\dots,L_{\mathrm{dec}}\}, event states 𝐨t(ℓ)\mathbf{o}_{t}^{(\ell)} are updated via:

𝐨t(ℓ)=𝐨t(ℓ−1)+CrossAttn⁡(WQ​𝐨t(ℓ−1),WK​𝐠m⁡(t),WV​𝐠m⁡(t))\mathbf{o}_{t}^{(\ell)}=\mathbf{o}_{t}^{(\ell-1)}+\mathrm{CrossAttn}\left(W_{Q}\mathbf{o}_{t}^{(\ell-1)},W_{K}\mathbf{g}_{m(t)},W_{V}\mathbf{g}_{m(t)}\right)

where m⁡(t)m(t) is the patch index for event tt. This injects global context into the event stream before a final causal Transformer yields representations 𝐨t\mathbf{o}_{t} for prediction.

Next-item scoring.

Hidden states 𝐨t\mathbf{o}_{t} are matched against the target item embedding 𝐞vt+1\mathbf{e}_{v_{t+1}} and a sampled negative 𝐞vt−\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}^{-}} via independent sigmoid scoring. We minimize the loss:

(4) ℒ=−∑(u,t):vt+1≠0[logσ(𝐨t⊤𝐞vt+1)+logσ(−𝐨t⊤𝐞vt−)],\mathcal{L}=-\sum_{(u,t):\,v_{t+1}\neq 0}\left[\log\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{o}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v_{t+1}}\right)+\log\sigma\!\left(-\mathbf{o}_{t}^{\top}\mathbf{e}_{v_{t}^{-}}\right)\right],

where σ⁡(⋅)\sigma(\cdot) is the sigmoid function and the sum is over all non-padding positions.

3. Experiments

3.1. Datasets

We evaluate DP-Rec on three datasets: ML-1M (Harper and Konstan, 2015), ML-10M-L (Harper and Konstan, 2015), and KuaiRand (Gao et al., 2022). Due to the scarcity of public long-horizon benchmarks, we curated ML-10M-Long (ML-10M-L), a long-sequence variant retaining only users with ≥500\geq 500 interactions from ML-10M. Following standard protocols (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Yang et al., 2024), we apply 5-core filtering and chronological sorting. For KuaiRand, we retain only clicked interactions following standard implicit feedback practice, yielding 4,473 average actions per user. We adopt a leave-one-out split, reserving the final and penultimate interactions for testing and validation, respectively. Preprocessed statistics are detailed in Table 2.

3.2. Baselines

  • •

    GRU4Rec (Hidasi et al., 2015a): A standard RNN-based baseline utilizing Gated Recurrent Units for sequential modeling.

  • •

    SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018): A representative and widely adopted self-attention architecture employing a causal (unidirectional) Transformer.

  • •

    HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024): A point-wise Transducer-based model incorporating relative temporal information. We evaluate it in a unimodal, causal configuration to maintain architectural parity.

  • •

    LONGER (Chai et al., 2025): A hierarchical baseline that compresses sequences into fixed-size blocks via an InnerTransformer, specifically designed for long-range dependency modeling.

3.3. Evaluation Metrics

We report widely used NDCG@K=[10, 20] and HR@K=[5, 10, 20]. Across all datasets, and for both validation and test, we adopt sampled evaluation: for each user we score the held-out target item against 1,0001{,}000 uniformly sampled negatives and rank it within the resulting 10011001-item candidate set. While the model is trained over all timesteps (Eq. 4), evaluation follows the leave-one-out protocol and scores a single held-out target per user. For each test user uu, rank⁡(yu)\operatorname{rank}(y_{u}) denotes the rank of the held-out target yuy_{u} among these 10011001 candidates under the model’s scores. We compute

NDCG⁡@​K\displaystyle\operatorname{NDCG}@K =1|𝒰|​∑u∈𝒰𝕀[rank(yu)≤K]log2⁡(rank⁡(yu)+1),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\frac{\mathbb{I}[\operatorname{rank}(y_{u})\leq K]}{\log_{2}(\operatorname{rank}(y_{u})+1)},
HR⁡@​K\displaystyle\operatorname{HR}@K =1|𝒰|∑u∈𝒰𝕀[rank(yu)≤K].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{U}|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{I}[\operatorname{rank}(y_{u})\leq K].

3.4. FLOPs Accounting

Inference efficiency is measured by FLOPs per forward pass, following (Hoffmann et al., 2022) but excluding non-arithmetic costs (normalization, residuals, and embedding lookup). For a Transformer with sequence length NN, context cc, hidden dimension dd, expansion dffd_{\mathrm{ff}}, and LblockL_{\mathrm{block}} layers, the base complexity is defined as:

(5) FLOPs⁡(N,c)=N​Lblock​(4​d2​dff+8​d2+2​d​(c+1)).\mathrm{FLOPs}(N,c)=NL_{\mathrm{block}}\left(4d^{2}d_{\mathrm{ff}}+8d^{2}+2d(c+1)\right).

The terms represent the feed-forward network, projections (Q/K/V/OQ/K/V/O), and attention aggregation, respectively. Per-user FLOPs are calculated using actual sequence lengths. We set dff=1d_{\mathrm{ff}}=1 across all models.

For SASRec, the quadratic causal context c=(N+1)/2c=(N+1)/2 yields:

(6) FLOPsSAS=N​Lblock​(4​d2​dff+8​d2+d⁡(N+1)).\mathrm{FLOPs}_{\mathrm{SAS}}=NL_{\mathrm{block}}(4d^{2}d_{\mathrm{ff}}+8d^{2}+d(N+1)).

HSTU utilizes the same backbone with a 1.1×1.1\times overhead factor to account for gating operations. LONGER with compression ratio rr and G=⌈N/r⌉G=\lceil N/r\rceil groups is modeled as the sum of inner-group encoding, cross-attention, and global self-attention:

(7) FLOPsLNG=G⋅FLOPs⁡(r,r)+2​N​G​d+FLOPs⁡(G,G).\mathrm{FLOPs}_{\mathrm{LNG}}=G\cdot\mathrm{FLOPs}(r,r)+2NGd+\mathrm{FLOPs}(G,G).
DP-Rec Complexity:

With MM latent patches, average patch size npn_{p}, boundary window wew_{e}, and local window ww, we decompose DP-Rec cost into boundary detection (fbbdf_{\mathrm{bbd}}), temporal latent modeling (flatentf_{\mathrm{latent}}), local encoding/decoding (flocf_{\mathrm{loc}}), and bridge cross-attention (fbrgf_{\mathrm{brg}}):

(8) FLOPsDP=N⁡(fbbd​(we)+flatent​(M)np+floc​(w)+fbrg).\mathrm{FLOPs}_{\mathrm{DP}}=N\left(f_{\mathrm{bbd}}(w_{e})+\frac{f_{\mathrm{latent}}(M)}{n_{p}}+f_{\mathrm{loc}}(w)+f_{\mathrm{brg}}\right).

Each component is instantiated via Eq. 10 using its respective architecture. Notably, the boundary detector cost is included in the total inference budget despite being frozen during primary training.

3.5. Implementation Details

Training Configuration

All models were implemented in PyTorch and trained on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (40GB). Following established benchmarks (Kang and McAuley, 2018; Hidasi et al., 2015a), we trained ML-1M and ML-10M-L for 500 epochs, while KuaiRand was trained for 200 epochs. We use Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10−310^{-3} and a batch size of 128. To control for confounding factors during hyperparameter optimization, we set dropout to 0.00.0 and disable L2L_{2} regularization. Best-performing checkpoints are selected based on the highest validation NDCG@10, evaluated every 10 epochs. We do not employ early stopping.

Evaluation Protocols

We adopt two complementary evaluation regimes:

  • •

    Headline Comparison: We report a single FLOPs-budgeted operating point per dataset, selected by the best validation NDCG@10 under the corresponding FLOPs budget (see Table 3).

  • •

    Pareto Frontier: We characterize the efficiency–quality trade-off by sweeping architectures for models whose inference cost can be varied naturally through sequence length or latent compression, namely SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018), HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024), LONGER (Chai et al., 2025), and DP-Rec—we perform a wide architecture and compression sweep to characterize the efficiency–quality frontier (see Figure 4).

Model Specifications

We adopt the training pipeline from (Huang, 2020) and model components from RecTools (MobileTeleSystems, 2024) for GRU4Rec and HSTU. LONGER is a custom implementation due to unavailability of open-source code. For DP-Rec, we implement the architecture as described in Section 2.

  • •

    Fixed-Horizon Models: SASRec and HSTU employ 3 blocks with hidden dimensions d∈{32,64}d\in\{32,64\}. The maximum input length NmaxN_{\max} is selected from {25,50,100,200}\{25,50,100,200\} for ML-1M and {25,50,100,250,500}\{25,50,100,250,500\} for KuaiRand and ML-10M-L. HSTU specifically enables relative-time and relative-position encodings to give it temporal information comparable to DP-Rec. GRU4Rec utilizes {1,3}\{1,3\} stacks with d=64d=64 and Nmax=50N_{\max}=50 for ML-1M and Nmax=100N_{\max}=100 for KuaiRand and ML-10M-L.

  • •

    Compression-Based Models: For LONGER and DP-Rec, the input horizon NrawN_{\text{raw}} and patch budget MM are swept across dataset-specific ranges: {100,200}\{100,200\} and {2,…,100}\{2,\dots,100\} for ML-1M, and {250,500}\{250,500\} and {2,…,250}\{2,\dots,250\} for KuaiRand and ML-10M-L. LONGER utilizes a 1-block inner and 3-block outer Transformer. DP-Rec employs a 1-block local encoder and a 3-block latent Transformer (d∈{16,32,64}d\in\{16,32,64\}); to maintain parameter parity with SASRec, FFN expansion layer is omitted. We evaluate both max-pooling and cross-attention (k=8k=8) for patch aggregation. The boundary detector is implemented as a 1-block Transformer with a minimal 8 hidden dimension across all datasets. Both boundary detector and temporal local encoder are implemented with we=w=32w_{e}=w=32 (see supplementary material for the full configuration details).

Unless otherwise stated, all models use ReLU activation, and all reported results correspond to the best validation-selected configuration for each model and dataset. Total FLOPs are computed post-hoc from the realized inference configurations on the test set to ensure a precise efficiency analysis.

3.6. Results

Table 3 compares all models at a matched, per-dataset inference budget: we fix the FLOPs budget to the SASRec configuration with the best validation NDCG@10 (a fixed horizon of Nmax=50N_{\max}=50 on ML-1M and 100100 on ML-10M-L and KuaiRand), and report every other model at its strongest validation-selected configuration within that budget. GRU4Rec is the sole exception: because its recurrent cost is largely insensitive to horizon and already sits within the budget, we report its overall best configuration. This design places fixed-horizon truncation and latent compression on equal computational footing, and under these conditions DP-Rec is the top performer on every dataset and metric. Since it can process 44–5×5\times longer histories at the same cost, it recovers signal that truncation discards, improving over the strongest baseline by +21.1%+21.1\% on ML-10M-L and +11.0%+11.0\% on KuaiRand in NDCG@10. Its advantage over LONGER, the fixed-block compression baseline, is largest on ML-1M (+24.8%+24.8\% NDCG@10) consistent with the advantage of aligning patch boundaries to behavioral shifts over uniform, static segmentation. Taken together, these results indicate that DP-Rec turns behavioral-driven compression into consistent gains across every dataset and metric we evaluate.

3.7. Model Efficiency

To analyze the utility–efficiency trade-off, we map test NDCG@10 against total inference FLOPs across all model configurations. We derive the Pareto frontier for each family by sorting configurations by ascending FLOPs (breaking ties with higher utility) and retaining only those whose NDCG@10 exceeds all lower-cost predecessors. This ensures every frontier point is non-dominated, representing the maximum achievable quality for any given computational budget. The plotted Pareto curves connect only these frontier points identifying non-dominated configurations for each model family.

Pareto Dominance and Efficiency Gains

As illustrated in Figure 4, DP-Rec (red curve) consistently defines or expands the Pareto frontier across all benchmarks, shifting the operational envelope toward the upper-left quadrant. This dominance is characterized by two primary phenomena:

  • •

    Iso-compute Quality Gains: At equivalent FLOP budgets, DP-Rec yields superior utility. For instance, on KuaiRand (Figure 4c), where at 1011.510^{11.5} FLOPs, DP-Rec achieves an NDCG@10 of ≈0.45\approx 0.45, maintaining a clear lead over the nearest baseline, LONGER.

  • •

    Iso-quality Efficiency Gains: Conversely, DP-Rec satisfies target utility levels at a substantially reduced computational footprint. Due to the log10\log_{10} scale of the x-axis, small horizontal shifts represent multifold reductions in FLOPs. For example, in ML-1M (Figure 4a), reaching an NDCG@10 of 0.220.22 requires ≈7×\approx 7\times fewer FLOPs with DP-Rec (≈109.5\approx 10^{9.5}) compared to fixed-horizon models like SASRec or HSTU (≈1010.3\approx 10^{10.3}).

Efficiency and Adaptive Data Distribution

The Pareto frontiers also reveal a dataset-dependent pattern: LONGER’s uniform, fixed-block compression is far more competitive on KuaiRand than on the MovieLens variants, and DP-Rec’s margin over it shrinks accordingly (from +24.8% on ML-1M to +21.1% on ML-10M-L to +11.0% on KuaiRand). We attribute this to how interaction structure differs across domains: KuaiRand is a dense, high-frequency short-video feed in which recent context is strongly predictive, so uniformly compressed representations still capture most of the relevant signal, whereas the MovieLens variants accumulate over long time spans with sparser, more diverse engagement, spreading informative interactions throughout the history where uniform compression more easily blurs them. DP-Rec’s adaptive boundaries preserve this dispersed signal, which is why its advantage over uniform compression is largest on the more heterogeneous MovieLens histories.

3.8. Ablations

Unless otherwise noted, all ablations fix the base architecture at Llat=3L_{\mathrm{lat}}=3, d=64d=64, Lloc=1L_{\mathrm{loc}}=1, dloc=32d_{\mathrm{loc}}=32, w=32w=32, k=8k=8, and M^=2\hat{M}=2.

3.8.1. Local Module Capacity

The local encoder and decoder facilitate long-horizon compression via sliding-window attention. To examine how local capacity affects quality and efficiency, we ablate hidden size (dlocd_{\mathrm{loc}}) and depth (LlocL_{\mathrm{loc}}) while fixing all other parameters to the base configuration above. Reducing dlocd_{\mathrm{loc}} to 16 causes substantial degradation across all datasets (−14.70%-14.70\%, −6.05%-6.05\%, −5.72%-5.72\%), confirming that a minimum local capacity is necessary for effective patch compression. Expanding to dloc=64d_{\mathrm{loc}}=64 yields meaningful gains on ML-1M (+6.75%+6.75\%) and ML-10M-L (+2.78%+2.78\%) and modest gains on KuaiRand (+0.85%+0.85\%), though at roughly 3.5×3.5\times the compute cost. Increasing depth reveals a dataset-dependent pattern: Lloc=2L_{\mathrm{loc}}=2 and Lloc=3L_{\mathrm{loc}}=3 cause mild degradation on ML-1M (−0.85%-0.85\%, −4.16%-4.16\%) and ML-10M-L (+2.15%+2.15\%, −2.00%-2.00\%), but provide marginal gains on KuaiRand (+0.34%+0.34\%, +0.89%+0.89\%), suggesting that denser interaction sequences can leverage deeper local context. Together, dloc=32d_{\mathrm{loc}}=32 with Lloc=1L_{\mathrm{loc}}=1 offers the best quality-efficiency trade-off across datasets, though higher capacity configurations may be worth exploring for dense, high-frequency domains.

3.8.2. Architectural Ablations

We evaluate the sensitivity of DP-Rec to local design choices under extreme compression (M^=2\hat{M}=2), fixing all other parameters to the base configuration above.

Time-RoPE removal causes consistent degradation across all datasets (Table 5), with losses of −9.83%-9.83\% and −5.75%-5.75\% on ML-1M and ML-10M-L, and a smaller −1.99%-1.99\% on KuaiRand, confirming that continuous temporal encoding is important for capturing interaction timing, particularly on sparser MovieLens sequences.

Cross-attention aggregator (kk, the number of latent queries per patch): its effect is consistently dataset-dependent at extreme compression. On ML-1M, removing cross-attention in favour of max-pooling yields +8.31%+8.31\%, and on KuaiRand it similarly yields +1.74%+1.74\%, suggesting that at M^=2\hat{M}=2 with only two coarse patches, max-pool aggregation is sufficient or preferable for both short and dense sequences. Only on ML-10M-L does cross-attention remain beneficial (−1.22%-1.22\% without it). Varying kk shows small, inconsistent effects across datasets at M^=2\hat{M}=2, with marginal gains for k=32k=32 on ML-1M (+2.86%+2.86\%) and near-neutral results elsewhere, confirming k=8k=8 as a reasonable default but suggesting cross-attention capacity matters more at higher patch budgets.

Sliding-window size (ww) exhibits a clear threshold effect: w=8w=8 causes substantial utility loss across all datasets (up to −12.60%-12.60\% on ML-1M and −8.29%-8.29\% on KuaiRand), as insufficient local context prevents accurate resolution of behavioral shifts. w=64w=64 yields consistent gains across all three datasets (+0.22%+0.22\%, +0.68%+0.68\%, +3.64%+3.64\%) but at higher computational cost; w=32w=32 offers the best efficiency trade-off.

3.8.3. Impact of Patching Scheme

To isolate whether DP-Rec’s gains stem from dynamic boundary placement rather than sequence compression alone, we vary only the boundary selection rule: Random (uniform random), Fixed (equal-sized blocks, matching LONGER’s chunking (Chai et al., 2025)), and Contrastive Entropy (CE) (boundaries at high-surprisal transitions; Section 2.2). We evaluate at M^=50\hat{M}=50 for ML-1M and M^=100\hat{M}=100 for ML-10M-L and KuaiRand, providing sufficient patch granularity for the three boundary rules to express meaningful behavioral differences. CE consistently outperforms both baselines across all three datasets (Table 6). Fixed improves over Random on all three datasets (+1.5%+1.5\%/+1.8%+1.8\%/+1.0%+1.0\% on ML-1M/ML-10M-L/KuaiRand) by preserving temporal locality. CE adds a further +4.2%+4.2\%/+2.4%+2.4\%/+2.7%+2.7\% over Fixed by aligning boundaries with genuine intent shifts, confirming that high-surprisal boundary detection captures meaningful behavioral transitions across all three domains. Note that these configurations are not constrained to the headline FLOPs budget and are thus not directly comparable to Table 3.

3.9. Sensitivity to Target Patch Budget

The target patch budget M^\hat{M} controls the bottleneck between local interaction processing and the temporal latent transformer. Table 7 reports test NDCG@10 at each budget, at fixed Nraw=50N_{\text{raw}}=50 for ML-1M and Nraw=100N_{\text{raw}}=100 for ML-10M-L and KuaiRand. Cross-attention aggregation is disabled for this ablation to isolate patch budget sensitivity from the confounding effect of cross-attention capacity becoming degenerate when k>npk>n_{p} at high M^\hat{M} (Section 3.8.2). Both ML-1M and KuaiRand peak at M^=50\hat{M}=50, while ML-10M-L continues to improve up to M^=250\hat{M}=250, consistent with its longer interaction histories requiring finer-grained segmentation. Despite this variation, DP-Rec is highly resilient to aggressive compression: even at M^=2\hat{M}=2 it retains ∼94%{\sim}94\% of peak NDCG@10 on ML-1M, ∼98%{\sim}98\% on ML-10M-L, and ∼96%{\sim}96\% on KuaiRand, confirming that the contrastive boundary detector packs the most salient behavioral shifts into very few patches.

4. Qualitative Analysis

Visualizations of interaction sequences in Figure 5 confirm that DP-Rec functions as an adaptive segmentation module, partitioning user histories into variable-length behavioral patches. We observe that contrastive entropy surprise serves as a robust proxy for these latent transitions: scores remain suppressed during thematically stable episodes, such as consistent genre engagement in ML-1M, allowing the local encoder to condense redundant interactions. Conversely, sharp entropy spikes occur during “out-of-distribution” events, including abrupt genre shifts or changes in interaction rhythm. This dynamic alignment ensures that latent representations are allocated according to behavioral complexity rather than fixed temporal intervals.

5. Limitations and Future Work

While DP-Rec demonstrates strong efficiency gains under FLOPs-matched comparisons, several limitations remain. First, a gap exists between theoretical complexity and practical throughput, as the patch aggregation kernels require further low-level optimization to match highly optimized fixed-length serving systems. Second, in our staged training pipeline, the boundary detector is pre-trained and frozen. While this approach to staged training is effective, learning patch boundaries jointly with the recommendation objective is a promising direction. Third, hardware constraints precluded study of ultra-long horizons (N > 500), where compression benefits may be even more pronounced. We hypothesize that richer multi-channel behavioral signals would provide more informative boundaries for contextual segmentation. More broadly, our contrastive-entropy detector is one effective instantiation of the boundary module, and identifying the best boundary-detection design (spanning alternative surprise signals, temporal cues, and training objectives) remains an open direction for future work.

6. Conclusions

In this study we introduced DP-Rec, a dynamic latent patching architecture with temporally adaptive boundary detection. DP-Rec couples item-level processing with explicit temporal modeling, combining temporal signals with contrastive entropy surprise to adaptively determine patch boundaries. This allows the model to overcome the quadratic constraints of standard Transformers while preserving high-fidelity representations of extended user histories. Experiments across three widely known public benchmarks confirm a superior computational efficiency–accuracy trade-off over both uncompressed and fixed-rate compression baselines, demonstrating that computation can follow the information density of user behavior rather than the arbitrary constraints of fixed boundaries. We invite future research to build upon this work to explore the potential of adaptive sequence modeling in recommender systems. 11 1 In preparing this paper, the authors utilized Gemini to improve the clarity, grammar, and presentation of the manuscript. No AI tools were used for model design, experimentation, or analysis; all technical contributions remain exclusively those of the authors.

Appendix A Relevant Work

A.1. Long Sequential Recommendation

Sequential recommendation has attracted substantial attention in both academia and industry (Katariya et al., 2025; Pancha et al., 2022; Hansen et al., 2020; Deng et al., 2025; Xin et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Xia et al., 2025; Guan et al., 2025; Xia et al., 2023; Zhai et al., 2024). Transformer based models, especially SASRec (Kang and McAuley, 2018) and BERT4Rec (Sun et al., 2019), have become foundational in this area by demonstrating the effectiveness of self attention for modeling user behavior sequences. These methods significantly advanced the state of the art over earlier sequential models such as GRU4Rec (Hidasi et al., 2015b), FPMC (Rendle et al., 2010), and CASER, as well as non sequential approaches including BPR-MF (Rendle et al., 2012) and NCF (He et al., 2017). Nevertheless, most existing methods are designed for relatively short or truncated interaction histories. Scaling these architectures to lifelong user logs is restricted not only by the quadratic complexity of self-attention but also by the increasing heterogeneity of user interests. These factors render assumptions of signal homogeneity and limited temporal scope increasingly unrealistic in large-scale settings (Zhou et al., 2026). Early work in this area focused primarily on explicit feedback, such as numerical ratings. Subsequent studies, however, established that Click-Through Rate (CTR) prediction—the estimation of a user’s probability of engagement—benefits from jointly modeling heterogeneous behavioral signals. Specifically, these models incorporate both positive signals, such as successful clicks, and negative signals, such as unclicked impressions where an item was exposed to the user but failed to elicit an interaction. In particular, DSTN (Ouyang et al., 2019), DFN (Xie et al., 2021), DIEN (Zhou et al., 2019), and XDM (Lv et al., 2022) demonstrated the importance of incorporating such multi-feedback information. Because implicit signals such as views and impressions are substantially more abundant than clicks, their inclusion greatly increases sequence length and makes full long-range sequence modeling computationally infeasible. To better exploit richer behavioral information, RACP (Fan et al., 2022) introduced a hierarchical attention architecture that captures both intra-page dependencies among co displayed items and inter-page interest transitions across sessions. Despite these advances, prior studies largely overlook the impact of sequence truncation in multi-feedback settings, where truncation can weaken cross-signal dependencies and limit the joint modeling of different feedback types. TEM4CTR (Zhang et al., 2023) addresses this issue through a three-stage framework that first retrieves unclicked records near clicked ones, then applies attention to identify relevant exposure information, and finally jointly extracts latent user interests from clicked and unclicked sequences for CTR prediction. Hence, recent practice increasingly favors integrating a broader range of user behavioral signals into recommendation models. While this enriches user representation, it also leads to substantial sequence length growth, thereby making efficient sequence processing a critical requirement.

A.2. Sequence Compression in RecSys

Under strict inference budget constraints, industrial RecSys often rely on staged compression pipelines to make long behavioral histories tractable. These include two stage retrieval methods such as TWIN (Chang et al., 2023), TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024), and SIM (Pi et al., 2020), pre trained embedding approaches such as PINNERFORMER (Pancha et al., 2022), SUM (Zhang et al., 2024b), DCE (Chitsazan et al., 2021), CoSeRNN (Hansen et al., 2020), and FinTRec (Katariya et al., 2025), as well as memory augmented methods such as LMN (Lu et al., 2025), Marm (Lv et al., 2024), MIMN (Pi et al., 2019). While these methods differ in design, they share a common goal of reducing sequence length before downstream modeling. For example, TWIN V2 (Si et al., 2024) compresses histories through clustering, whereas TWIN (Chang et al., 2023), UBR4CTR (Qin et al., 2020), SIM (Pi et al., 2020), and TransAct (Xia et al., 2023) retrieve a target relevant subset of interactions followed by lightweight self attention. Although effective in reducing computation, these strategies often sacrifice signal fidelity. Because compression is performed upstream, they are typically not optimized end-to-end with downstream item relevance, and may therefore miss important real-time behavioral signals (Xia et al., 2025). This separation between compression and recommendation also limits the model’s ability to preserve the fine-grained structure of long behavioral histories. In addition, staged designs introduce operational overhead by requiring coordination between upstream retraining and downstream serving. Recent work has attempted to address these limitations more directly. TransAct V2 (Xia et al., 2025) demonstrates the benefit of combining lifelong histories with real time signals, but restricts the lifelong component to high signal explicit interactions, keeping the final sequence length at approximately 10210^{2} and still discarding fine-grained information. Another direction explores generative architectures such as HSTU (Zhai et al., 2024), though these often require extremely large models and substantial compute budgets (Xia et al., 2023). LONGER (Chai et al., 2025) reduces computation through fixed window token merging followed by a lightweight Transformer over adjacent tokens. While this lowers FLOPs without hurting baseline accuracy, fixed-rate merging cannot adapt to the uneven information density of heterogeneous user behaviors. Recently, PerRec (Zhang et al., 2025b) introduced learnable tokens for sequence compression; however, it still relied on a fixed set of learnable tokens. In contrast, DP-Rec processes raw long-range sequences directly with Transformer architecture, reducing reliance on aggressive upfront compression and fixed set of assumed windows and/or learnable tokens.

A.3. Sequence Compressions in Other Domains

Recent research has increasingly focused on relaxing fixed-length constraints through adaptive or multi-scale segmentation strategies. Frameworks such as MSPatch (Cao et al., 2025) and HDMixer (Huang et al., 2024) leverage multi-resolution patching and extendable interpolation, respectively, while MOIRAI (Woo et al., 2024) determines patch granularity within the frequency domain. Other approaches address sequence non-stationarity and irregular intervals; for example, AdaPatch (Liu et al., 2025) introduces patch-level normalization, and APN (Liu et al., 2026) employs time-aware aggregation driven by data-density regularization. More granular architectures like SRSNet (Wu et al., 2025) and TimeMosaic (Ding et al., 2026) utilize selective reassembly or motif-based adaptation to enhance representation efficiency and decoding specialization. EntroPE(Abeywickrama et al., 2025), recently explored application of BLT to timeseries demonstrating strong efficiency and performance gains.

Appendix B Temporal Rotary Positional Embeddings (Time-RoPE)

To encode interaction rhythms, we adapt Rotary Positional Embeddings (Su et al., 2024) to absolute timestamps TtT_{t}. For a latent vector 𝐱∈ℝd\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the transformation ℛ⁡(𝐱,Tt)\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x},T_{t}) rotates d/2d/2 dimension pairs in the query-key space:

(9) ℛ⁡(𝐱,Tt)=𝐱⊙cos⁡(𝚯​Tt)+𝐱~⊙sin⁡(𝚯​Tt)\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{x},T_{t})=\mathbf{x}\odot\cos(\mathbf{\Theta}T_{t})+\mathbf{\tilde{x}}\odot\sin(\mathbf{\Theta}T_{t})

where 𝚯={θi=10000−2i/d}i=1d/2\mathbf{\Theta}=\{\theta_{i}=10000^{-2i/d}\}_{i=1}^{d/2} are the inverse frequencies. This makes the attention score between two interactions at times TtT_{t} and Tt′T_{t^{\prime}} a function of their time lag (Tt−Tt′)(T_{t}-T_{t^{\prime}}), giving both the local and latent Transformers a continuous, density-aware sense of behavioral timing.

Appendix C Lemma - Patch-count calibration under distinct scores

The following lemma formalizes the calibration property of the proposed thresholding rule under an idealized no-tie condition. Specifically, it shows that when all valid surprise scores are distinct, selecting the threshold as the kk-th largest valid score yields exactly the intended number of detected boundaries, and hence matches the target average patch budget up to rounding. The result is purely combinatorial and serves to justify the thresholding mechanism, rather than the semantic quality of the resulting boundaries.

Lemma C.1 (Patch-count calibration under distinct scores).

Let ϕ∈ℝB×N\phi\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N} denote the surprise scores, 𝛍∈{0,1}B×N\boldsymbol{\mu}\in\{0,1\}^{B\times N} the padding mask, and Φ={ϕu,t∣𝛍u,t=1}\Phi=\{\phi_{u,t}\mid\boldsymbol{\mu}_{u,t}=1\} the multiset of valid scores. Let M^\hat{M} be the target average number of patches, N¯=|Φ|/B\bar{N}=|\Phi|/B the average sequence length, and Meff=min⁡(M^,N¯)M_{\mathrm{eff}}=\min(\hat{M},\bar{N}). Define the boundary budget as:

k=round⁡((Meff−1)​B).k=\mathrm{round}((M_{\mathrm{eff}}-1)B).

Assume all values in Φ\Phi are distinct and 0≤k≤|Φ|0\leq k\leq|\Phi|. Let τ\tau be the kk-th largest element of Φ\Phi, and 𝚪u,t=𝕀[ϕu,t≥τ]⋅𝛍u,t\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{u,t}=\mathbb{I}[\phi_{u,t}\geq\tau]\cdot\boldsymbol{\mu}_{u,t}. Then the total number of detected boundaries is exactly kk, and the total number of patches is:

Total Patches=k+B=round⁡(Meff​B).\text{Total Patches}=k+B=\mathrm{round}(M_{\mathrm{eff}}B).

Consequently, the average number of patches per sequence equals MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}}.

Proof.

Since all scores in Φ\Phi are distinct, the kk-th largest value τ\tau is unique. By definition of the kk-th order statistic, there are exactly kk elements in Φ\Phi with ϕu,t≥τ\phi_{u,t}\geq\tau. Thus the total boundary count is:

∑u=1B∑t=1N𝚪u,t=k.\sum_{u=1}^{B}\sum_{t=1}^{N}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{u,t}=k.

Each sequence u∈{1,…,B}u\in\{1,\dots,B\} is partitioned into Mu=γu+1M_{u}=\gamma_{u}+1 patches, where γu=∑t𝚪u,t\gamma_{u}=\sum_{t}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}_{u,t} is its boundary count. The total number of patches across the batch is:

∑u=1BMu=∑u=1B(γu+1)=(∑u=1Bγu)+B=k+B.\sum_{u=1}^{B}M_{u}=\sum_{u=1}^{B}(\gamma_{u}+1)=\left(\sum_{u=1}^{B}\gamma_{u}\right)+B=k+B.

Substituting k=round⁡((Meff−1)​B)=round⁡(Meff​B−B)k=\mathrm{round}((M_{\mathrm{eff}}-1)B)=\mathrm{round}(M_{\mathrm{eff}}B-B) and using that BB is an integer:

k+B=round⁡(Meff​B)−B+B=round⁡(Meff​B).k+B=\mathrm{round}(M_{\mathrm{eff}}B)-B+B=\mathrm{round}(M_{\mathrm{eff}}B).

Dividing by BB yields the average patch count MeffM_{\mathrm{eff}}, which equals the target M^\hat{M} whenever the average sequence length N¯\bar{N} is sufficient. ∎

Appendix D Robustness to Item Popularity Tiers

The analysis of recommendation utility across item frequency tiers reveals that while all models benefit from increased interaction density, their ability to handle "tail" versus "head" items varies significantly. Across all three datasets, we observe a monotonic increase in NDCG@10 as item frequency rises, confirming that higher-resolution signals for popular items naturally facilitate more accurate predictions. DP-Rec consistently establishes the performance ceiling across the entire popularity spectrum. Specifically, in low-frequency bins (<25<25 interactions), DP-Rec exhibits greater resilience than standard baselines, suggesting that its adaptive boundary detection effectively extracts meaningful patterns even from sparse interaction data where fixed-horizon models like SASRec and HSTU struggle to isolate a clear signal.

In the high-frequency regime (>100>100 interactions), the advantage of compression-based architectures becomes even more pronounced. In ML-10M-Long and KuaiRand, both DP-Rec and LONGER significantly outperform fixed-horizon baselines. This indicates that for popular items, relevant behavioral context is likely distributed across a much longer temporal window; while fixed-horizon models are limited by rigid truncation, the adaptive patching of DP-Rec allows it to aggregate information from the entire user history without signal dilution. Notably, in KuaiRand, LONGER performs exceptionally well, closely trailing DP-Rec, whereas in ML-1M, DP-Rec maintains a wider margin over all competitors in the mid-to-head tiers. Collectively, these results demonstrate that DP-Rec provides a robust architectural advantage that scales effectively from sparse tail items to dense head items, outperforming both traditional attention-based models and uniform compression strategies.

Appendix E Performance across Temporal Lag Bins

Temporal analysis across the experimental suite clarifies how the distribution of target signals modulates model performance over time. In ML-1M and KuaiRand, we observe a significant recency bias, where predictive utility for all models effectively collapses by the most distal bin (T3). In these scenarios, DP-Rec demonstrates superior peak performance in the immediate temporal bin (T1), indicating its efficacy in capturing high-entropy signals within recent interactions. However, model behavior diverges in the transition to T2: while LONGER maintains a slight edge in ML-1M, it suffers a catastrophic collapse to zero in KuaiRand, whereas HSTU exhibits higher middle-range robustness. This suggests that while uniform compression or fixed horizons can occasionally capture specific temporal windows, they are inherently prone to failure when the underlying signal density shifts. The results for ML-10M-Long provide the most compelling evidence for DP-Rec’s architectural advantage in long-range scenarios. Unlike the other datasets, ML-10M-Long exhibits remarkable signal persistence, with significant utility maintained even in the T3 bin. Here, DP-Rec consistently defines the performance ceiling across the entire temporal spectrum, maintaining a nearly flat and dominant trajectory compared to baselines. Its ability to preserve distal signals—while models like SASRec and LONGER struggle to close the gap—confirms that the entropy-driven boundary detector successfully identifies and retains informative behavioral shifts regardless of their sequence position. Collectively, these results highlight that while baseline models are often constrained by a dataset’s inherent temporal decay, DP-Rec’s adaptive patching provides a robust efficiency advantage across both high-recency and signal-persistent environments.

Long-sequence recommendation is particularly relevant in sparse and long-tail settings, where a user’s older interactions may still contain useful preference signal. We therefore analyze performance stratified by item popularity to assess whether DP-Rec is especially beneficial for long-tail recommendation. Because adaptive patching preserves informative intent transitions rather than truncating the sequence uniformly, DP-Rec demonstrates gains across all the item popularity cohorts(refer Figure 6).
